units.title: Economic rights & patient mobility
units.intro: Start with the legal route, not with a promise of reimbursement. This guide follows the lecture from EU integration to the moving patient.
review: The lecture presents two economic paths: removing barriers and harmonising national rules.
Primary and secondary EU law are different levels, not competing synonyms.
A regulation and a directive do not operate in the same way in national law.
Receiving a health service across a border is part of the lecture’s freedom-of-services analysis.
Prior authorisation, waiting times and reimbursement require separate questions.
Article 56 case law, Regulation 883/2004 and Directive 2011/24 are distinct legal bases.
Do not treat the EHIC as permission to travel for planned treatment.

sections.title: Two paths from integration to health policy
paragraphs: The lecture starts with economic integration and then adds the political, human-rights and values dimensions. In the market perspective, one path challenges national barriers to free movement. Another creates common standards through harmonisation. They can both influence health care, but they do different work: removing an obstacle is not the same as designing a shared rule.

Before analysing a problem, identify what moves: goods, a worker, a self-employed provider, the recipient of a service, or the service itself. The lecture’s active/passive services distinction is useful: patient mobility is the recipient crossing the border. This does not turn every health-policy dispute into a cross-border market case.

sections.title: Read the instrument before applying the rule
paragraphs: Treaties and the Charter form the primary-law layer in the slides. Regulations, directives and decisions sit in the secondary-law layer. The lecture contrasts a regulation’s direct applicability with a directive’s implementation through national law. Its diagram also flags the special question of an unimplemented directive and rights against a Member State; do not assume every directive works identically in every dispute.

Competence is a separate question. The slides distinguish exclusive, shared, and supporting competences. Their point is not that health is untouched by the EU, but that the legal basis and type of intervention must be identified. The EEA discussion similarly asks the reader to examine relevance and incorporation rather than assume that every EU measure applies everywhere in Europe.

sections.title: Watts: why the waiting list matters
paragraphs: In the lecture’s Watts example, a patient with hip arthritis and continuing pain seeks treatment outside her home system. The legal discussion connects an individual’s clinical circumstances to the system’s authorisation and planning rules. A waiting list is not simply a calendar number: the lecture emphasises medical assessment rather than an exclusively administrative view of delay.

A useful study sequence is: identify the treatment and home entitlement; identify the legal route; examine whether authorisation is required; examine the reasons for refusal or delay; then consider the reimbursement rule and review procedure. This is an original study scaffold based on the lecture, not a complete eligibility test.

sections.title: Three legal bases; do not collapse their conditions
paragraphs: The course identifies Treaty freedom-of-services case law, social-security coordination under Regulation 883/2004, and the cross-border healthcare directive. The directive also discusses information, national contact points, prescriptions and cooperation. The slides later distinguish developments in health technology assessment and health data from the original directive’s structure.

Supplementary clarification: the public-authority references distinguish necessary care during a temporary stay using the EHIC from authorised planned care using the S2 route. The directive route commonly involves paying first and applying for reimbursement under the home system’s conditions. Local cost-sharing, public-system affiliation, authorisation and eligibility still matter. The lecture’s compact route chart should not be read as “no one ever pays upfront” or “EHIC covers planned treatment”.

sections.title: Competence is not the same question as a patient’s right
paragraphs: The lecture asks two different questions: which level may adopt legislation, and what rights a person can invoke in a cross-border situation. Its competence chart distinguishes exclusive EU fields, shared fields, and support, coordination or supplementation. Health appears in more than one part of that chart: protection and improvement of human health is distinguished from common safety concerns in public health. Internal-market powers are also relevant. A useful answer therefore identifies the particular activity rather than treating every health-related measure as belonging to one undifferentiated competence.

The two economic paths then explain different mechanisms of change. Challenging a national barrier can remove an obstacle in a particular legal setting; harmonisation actively establishes common standards through legislation. Neither mechanism, as presented here, means that all national health systems have been replaced. Study task: explain which mechanism is being used before discussing its consequences for patients, providers or national planning. This is a reading framework, not an independent determination that a proposed policy has a valid legal basis.
sections.locator: Economic rights, PDF pp. 4, 8, 11 and 17

sections.title: Turn the case-law chart into a structured analysis
paragraphs: The patient-mobility chart brings several questions together. Start with the treatment that the home system covers, then identify any relevant referral or other general conditions. Next separate the possibility of requiring prior authorisation from the reasons for granting or refusing it. The lecture associates hospital care and major medical equipment with planning concerns, while its non-hospital example is treated differently. That contrast should be read within the chart’s case-law setting rather than turned into an unconditional promise about every contemporary treatment abroad.

For waiting lists, the Watts discussion directs attention to a medical assessment of the patient’s circumstances, not merely an administrative place in the queue. The chart also connects authorisation procedures with accessibility, objectivity and review, and distinguishes treatment costs from travel and accommodation. A strong short answer keeps these questions separate: coverage, procedure, clinically acceptable delay, and the relevant reimbursement limit. The examples do not supply an individual patient’s clinical record, national rules or insurer decision, so those facts must remain unresolved rather than invented.
sections.locator: Economic rights, PDF pp. 21–26, especially p. 25

sections.title: What the Directive adds beyond paying a bill
paragraphs: The lecture’s outline of Directive 2011/24/EU contains more than reimbursement provisions. It separates responsibilities of the Member State of treatment from those of the Member State of affiliation, identifies national contact points, and presents cooperation concerning prescriptions, European reference networks, rare diseases, eHealth and health technology assessment. This organisation is useful: patient mobility requires usable information and coordination as well as a route for paying for treatment. A reimbursement answer alone would miss those institutional dimensions of the lecture.

The later slide on selected topics also shows why the date and version of an instrument matter. It annotates the original outline with later instruments concerning health technology assessment, health data and reporting. Treat the earlier outline as a guide to the development of the framework, not a guarantee that every provision remains unchanged. The EEA discussion is a further distinct layer: the course introduces EEA relevance and EFTA case law, but it does not make EU membership, EEA participation and every individual entitlement interchangeable.
sections.locator: Economic rights, PDF pp. 28–33

units.title: Human rights & the right to health care
units.intro: Separate the institution, the protected right and the justification for interference. Then connect rights to services through AAAQ.
review: Human rights, fundamental rights and citizenship rights are related but not interchangeable terms.
The EU Charter and the ECHR belong to different institutional systems.
Article 35 concerns access to preventive care and medical treatment, with national conditions.
AAAQ means availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality.
Accessibility includes financial, physical, information and non-discrimination dimensions.
Respect, protect and fulfil identify different state obligations.
Legal permission for a vaccination policy is not the same question as whether it should be chosen.

sections.title: Which document and which court?
paragraphs: The lecturer distinguishes citizenship rights tied to nationality, fundamental rights by their foundational importance, and human rights held by human beings. The EU, the Council of Europe and the UN are not interchangeable sources. Name the document before interpreting the right.

The lecture pairs the EU Charter with the Court of Justice in Luxembourg and the European Convention on Human Rights with the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. It notes similarities in interpretation without merging the two systems. An answer that cites Article 8 ECHR should therefore not attribute that provision to the EU Charter.

sections.title: From a broad idea of health to a usable framework
paragraphs: The WHO material in the lecture treats health more broadly than absence of disease. General Comment 14 provides a framework for examining the services and conditions needed to realise the right. Availability asks whether sufficient functioning provision exists. Accessibility asks whether people can reach and use it without discriminatory, geographical, financial or information barriers.

Acceptability asks whether care respects ethics and cultural contexts. Quality asks whether services are scientifically and medically appropriate. These are complementary checks, not a league table. A well-equipped clinic can still be inaccessible, while a nearby affordable service can still have a quality problem.

sections.title: Who must do what?
paragraphs: The slides move beyond a simple positive-versus-negative rights split. Respect concerns avoiding interference with enjoyment of the right. Protect concerns preventing interference by third parties. Fulfil concerns the legislative, administrative, budgetary and other measures needed to make the right effective.

Article 35 is presented as a healthcare entitlement connected to national law and practice, not an unlimited guarantee of any desired treatment. Supplementary scope note: the Commission’s public explanation says that national authorities are bound by the Charter when implementing EU law. A study answer should state the scope question rather than imply that Article 35 decides every domestic dispute by itself.

sections.title: Vavřička: keep the reasoning and the facts together
paragraphs: The lecture’s analysis follows scope, interference and justification under Article 8 ECHR. Justification involves a legal basis, a legitimate aim and necessity in a democratic society, including proportionality. It discusses protection of vulnerable children and solidarity alongside individual physical integrity.

The safeguards and circumstances matter: no vaccine was administered against the applicants’ will, exemptions and review procedures were relevant, and the sanctions were examined in context. The case is a structured example concerning childhood vaccination, not a blanket answer for every disease, population or mandate. The later discussion deliberately changes the question from whether a policy can be mandatory to whether it should be.

sections.title: Široká and Padova: why the court may not reach the merits
paragraphs: In Široká, the lecture describes a challenge connected with a parent’s refusal to vaccinate a child. The important lesson is jurisdiction: the Charter applies to Member States when they implement Union law, and the Court did not obtain a sufficient EU-law basis to answer the questions presented. That procedural result is not a substantive judgment that every vaccination duty is justified. First establish the legal connection; only then examine the relevant right and any interference with it.

The Padova discussion concerns a nurse suspended after refusing a national vaccination requirement. The slides stress inadequacies in the referring court’s information and the link between the questions and the dispute. They also distinguish an authorisation to market a vaccine from a legal obligation to receive it. When comparing these cases, explain the procedural issue separately from the public-health controversy. Do not combine a jurisdictional limit, an inadmissible reference and a full proportionality analysis into the single statement that the court approved mandatory vaccination.
sections.locator: Human rights, PDF pp. 33–36

sections.title: Vavřička: reconstruct the sequence, not just the outcome
paragraphs: The Vavřička slides organise Article 8 analysis as scope, interference and justification. Physical integrity falls within private life; recognising an interference begins the analysis rather than ending it. Justification is then considered through legal accessibility and foreseeability, a legitimate aim, and necessity in a democratic society. The protection of others includes children unable to receive a vaccine themselves. The margin of appreciation concerns the space for national decision-making, but the slides also emphasise continuing judicial review.

The specific safeguards matter to that assessment: no vaccination was forcibly administered to the applicants, medical contraindications were considered, sanctions were discussed, and administrative and judicial remedies existed. The source also addresses safety monitoring and the relevance of compensation. These facts should accompany any summary of the reasoning. A different disease, population, sanction or implementation method would require its own analysis. Finally, distinguish the legal question of whether a measure may be justified from the ethical question of whether it should be the preferred policy.
sections.locator: Human rights, PDF pp. 41–46

sections.title: Use AAAQ alongside respect, protect and fulfil
paragraphs: AAAQ describes dimensions of the service or health system: sufficient provision, practical accessibility, cultural and ethical acceptability, and scientific and medical quality. Respect, protect and fulfil instead organise the duties of the responsible authority. They are complementary frameworks, not rival lists. The lecture describes respect as refraining from interference, protection as addressing interference by others, and fulfilment as taking measures towards realisation. Do not classify a problem under one heading and assume that this already identifies every required action.

Original application: a functioning clinic may still be unaffordable, hard to reach and unable to provide information patients can use. These are different accessibility barriers, not proof that the clinic does not exist. A separate question is which actor can change fees, transport, communication or provider behaviour. This example illustrates how to link a barrier to an obligation; it is not a case from the lecturer. The broad WHO framing of health also explains why a discussion limited to the hospital building would omit social and other determinants identified in the course.
sections.locator: Human rights, PDF pp. 20–25

units.title: Non-discrimination: analyse the difference
units.intro: Begin with comparability, then identify the ground, the field and the relevant legal framework. Avoid jumping directly to a verdict.
review: Different treatment of comparable situations can raise a discrimination issue.
Identical treatment of relevantly different situations can also raise an issue.
Direct discrimination expressly uses a protected ground; indirect discrimination can use a neutral-looking criterion.
Ground and field both matter: a rule for employment is not automatically a rule for every health service.
The short summary’s examples depend on evidence and context.
A legitimate objective does not remove the need to examine proportionality.
Migration-related health entitlements differ by legal status and special needs.

sections.title: A disciplined sequence for analysis
paragraphs: The lecture starts with comparison. Ask which people or situations are being compared, which characteristics are relevant and what treatment differs. Next identify the ground, such as nationality or sex, and the setting, such as work or access to services. Then identify the applicable instrument. A statement that something feels unfair is a starting concern, not the completed legal analysis.

The short summary identifies three paths: economic free-movement rights, non-discrimination directives and human-rights protection. They have different scopes. The Charter’s broader list of grounds does not make the field and application questions disappear.

sections.title: Direct and indirect: look beyond the wording
paragraphs: Direct discrimination explicitly uses the ground in the decision. Indirect discrimination may arise from a neutral-looking criterion that disadvantages a protected group. In the short summary’s staff-event example, full-time priority can raise a sex-discrimination issue if evidence shows the relevant unequal pattern of part-time work. That factual condition must not be removed from the explanation.

The language example similarly distinguishes a sufficient command of the language for the actual job from a demand for perfection that is unnecessary for its tasks. The study lesson is to examine the requirement and its effects, not to declare every language requirement unlawful.

sections.title: The field of the directive is part of the answer
paragraphs: The deck contrasts racial or ethnic origin under Directive 2000/43, employment and occupation under Directive 2000/78, sex equality in goods and services under Directive 2004/113, and employment equality under Directive 2006/54. Its matrix is a teaching device for seeing differences of coverage.

A blank area in that matrix should not be turned into a claim that no other legal protection exists. Nor should the student apply an employment directive to a different setting without explaining why it is relevant. The slides’ reproductive-technology examples show why the precise ground and instrument change the reasoning.

sections.title: Migration and justification: preserve the distinctions
paragraphs: The detailed slides distinguish beneficiaries of international protection, applicants, temporary protection, long-term residence and people pending return. They quote equal eligibility conditions for beneficiaries of international protection, additional protections for children and special reception needs, and emergency and essential treatment rules in other contexts.

The deck’s final summary is broader and less detailed than these earlier slides. This guide follows the status-specific passages rather than reducing every group to emergency treatment only. The short summary also discusses public-health justification, evidence and necessity; the availability of a justification depends on the relevant rule, not on a general permission to discriminate. Detailed current application and national implementation require the official texts.

sections.title: The ground–field–instrument test
paragraphs: A claim needs more precision than “two people were treated differently”. The lecture links nationality and product origin to economic freedoms, distinguishes the Treaty’s nationality provision from other protected grounds, and presents several non-discrimination directives. For each problem, write down the proposed ground, the field of activity, and the instrument being invoked. A rule about employment does not automatically govern every service, and the existence of a broad Charter list does not remove the need to establish its scope of application.

The source distinguishes racial or ethnic origin under Directive 2000/43, employment-related protection under Directive 2000/78, sex equality in goods and services under Directive 2004/113, and sex equality in employment under Directive 2006/54. It specifically identifies healthcare in the racial-equality framework. These distinctions make a useful reading map, not an exhaustive account of every applicable rule. Where a slide lists a reform or a proposal, retain that status and consult the original instrument before asserting that the entire legal framework has changed.
sections.locator: Non-discrimination, PDF pp. 15–22; short summary, PDF p. 2

sections.title: Why evidence and a comparator change the answer
paragraphs: The short summary’s staff-event example uses full-time work as an apparently neutral priority rule. Its explanation is conditional: evidence that the rule disproportionately affects women can support an indirect sex-discrimination analysis. The text does not say that all full-time/part-time distinctions have the same effect. Identify who is disadvantaged, why the comparison is relevant, and what information supports the claimed connection. Intent to discriminate and the effects of a rule are different evidential questions.

The language example likewise asks whether the required level is necessary for the actual job. Some command of a language may be needed; a demand for perfect fluency may be excessive for the tasks described. The summary then considers objective justification and proportionality. A useful answer tests whether the measure can achieve the legitimate aim and whether a less restrictive alternative could do so. This is an original organisation of the supplied reasoning, not a general permission to justify every form of direct discrimination on any convenient ground.
sections.locator: Non-discrimination short summary, PDF pp. 1–4

sections.title: Keep reproductive and migration examples legally distinct
paragraphs: The reproductive examples show why the right claimed and the applicable definition matter. The Mayr discussion distinguishes protection under the pregnant-workers framework from possible sex-equality protection. The D and Z discussions concern the position of a commissioning mother and particular maternity-leave or equality claims. These are not presented as one general decision about whether assisted reproduction is morally acceptable. Study the issue, the relevant instrument and the limited conclusion separately; the source does not provide a current country-by-country guide to reproductive rights.

The migration section also distinguishes legal categories. The slides on beneficiaries of international protection describe healthcare under the same eligibility conditions as nationals; the reception-conditions slide separately addresses applicants, children and special reception needs. Other slides concern temporary protection, long-term residence and return. The deck’s final summary is much more compressed than these detailed provisions. Preserve both the existence of that broad summary and the specific distinctions: it would be misleading to turn the entire section into a single emergency-care entitlement for all migrants.
sections.locator: Non-discrimination, PDF pp. 24–29 (printed slide labels 27–35)

units.title: Ethics, EU values & health values
units.intro: Understand the vocabulary before using a value to defend a policy. Then ask what practical duties and safeguards follow.
review: Ethics is reflective inquiry; morality includes norms of conduct shared in a social setting.
Values are more abstract than action-guiding principles.
Article 2 TEU values and the 2006 health-system values have different legal status.
The health values are universality, access to good-quality care, equity and solidarity.
Operating principles connect values to quality, safety, evidence, participation and redress.
Personal values and values people associate with the EU are different survey constructs.
The historical Eurobarometer figures are not current cohort or population statistics.

sections.title: Ethics, morality, values and principles
paragraphs: The lecture places ethics within practical philosophy and presents morality as shared norms of right and wrong conduct. Ethical reflection can evaluate a prevailing norm rather than merely repeat it. Values express broad commitments, whereas principles give more concrete guidance for decision-making and action.

The lecture’s biomedical principles include autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice. Its legal and health-system principles partly overlap with ethical reasoning but are not identical to it. To say that a policy advances a value is therefore not yet to specify its legal effect or how it should be implemented.

sections.title: Two layers of values
paragraphs: The Article 2 TEU discussion concerns the Union’s foundational values, including dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights. The 2006 health-system discussion identifies universality, access to good-quality care, equity and solidarity. The lecture distinguishes binding primary law from non-binding health-minister conclusions.

The Council text connects equity to access according to need and solidarity to financing arrangements that sustain accessibility. It also recognises variation between national systems. A shared value does not prescribe one identical insurance design for all countries.

sections.title: Make the value operational
paragraphs: The operating principles include quality and safety, evidence and ethics, patient involvement, redress, and privacy and confidentiality. They help turn a general aspiration into a question about delivery: what information will patients receive, how can they participate, how is risk monitored, and how can an error be challenged?

Original reflection prompt: a service is formally open to everyone but requires complex online registration. Which accessibility and participation questions should be asked? The sources provide the concepts; they do not provide an official answer to this invented scenario.

sections.title: Read the survey before reading the bars
paragraphs: The deck contains separate Eurobarometer charts for personal values and for values associated with the EU. They are not measuring the same thing. The charts refer to historical survey waves and note that respect for the planet was added in 2019.

For revision, record the question, wave, population and available categories before comparing results. Do not use these charts to claim what the current EU-HEM cohort believes. This study edition does not reproduce or extrapolate the original chart values.

sections.title: Read the values diagram from abstract commitments to action
paragraphs: The diagram on page 29 places common EU values and health-specific values above more concrete ethical, legal and operational principles, with trust as an overarching goal. It separately names autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice, alongside legal principles such as transparency, proportionality and responsibility. This is a conceptual arrangement: it helps explain why stating a broad value is not the same as describing what a service should actually do. The diagram does not supply a numerical formula for balancing all principles.

Original application: a proposed digital appointment system could claim to promote equity, but the claim needs an operational explanation. Accessible information, a non-digital alternative and a way to challenge an error are possible design responses to analyse, not requirements asserted by the slide itself. Name the value, identify the practical principle, explain the action, and disclose a remaining conflict. The purpose is to develop reasoning that a classmate can question, rather than decorate a policy with a list of values that never influence its design.
sections.locator: Values and ethics, PDF pp. 8–9 and 29–30

sections.title: Ethical disagreement does not disappear at the border
paragraphs: The lecture opens its ethics discussion by revisiting sensitive issues and the distribution of competence. It then uses recitals from the patient-mobility directive to show legal references to ethical choices and professional duties. The example is not that economic integration has erased all moral disagreement. Rather, the course places law and ethics in a relationship mediated by values and human rights. The same healthcare activity can therefore raise an internal-market question and an ethical question without those questions being identical.

The repetition of human obligations adds a further perspective. A rights-based statement asks what a person should receive or be allowed to do; a duty-focused statement asks who must act and how. In an original seminar answer, follow a claim such as “patients should be involved” with an account of who provides information, who makes the decision, and how the patient’s contribution can matter. The lecture provides this distinction in orientation; it does not give an official answer to every ethical controversy raised in discussion.
sections.locator: Values and ethics, PDF pp. 3–5 and 11–15

sections.title: Surveys, legal commitments and recommendations are different evidence
paragraphs: The Eurobarometer slides distinguish values respondents personally hold from values they associate with the EU. A survey finding describes answers to a question; it is not itself the legal source of the Union’s values. The charts also use historical waves and flag the introduction of “respect for the planet” as a response category in 2019. When comparing bars, preserve the survey question, wave, population and available answer categories. Do not interpret a newly introduced category as evidence that nobody cared about it in earlier years.

The legal-status distinction is equally important. The lecture presents Article 2 TEU as binding primary law and the 2006 health-values conclusions as non-binding soft law. Soft law can still structure discussion and expectations, but its status should not be silently upgraded. A defensible paragraph can therefore distinguish three statements: what people report valuing, what a legal text establishes, and what policymakers are urged to pursue. These may support each other, but they require different evidence and do not answer the same question.
sections.locator: Values and ethics, PDF pp. 17–21 and 24–27

units.title: Bismarck & Beveridge: a comparison framework
units.intro: Use the models as a first map. The assigned country readings then explain the real institutions, incentives and access barriers.
review: The course groups the Netherlands and Austria under Bismarck, and Italy and Norway under Beveridge.
The teaching models contrast social insurance and taxation as organising ideas.
Separate financing, pooling, purchasing and provision when reading a system.
Public financing does not imply that every provider is publicly owned.
Population coverage does not by itself establish equal or timely access.
Country indicators require their own year, unit and denominator.
The country sessions ask about both system characteristics and the challenges of patient mobility.

sections.title: What the course models do—and do not—tell us
paragraphs: The organizational slides group four countries into two broad families and show a textbook comparison of the ideal types. Social insurance is the organising idea on the Bismarck side; taxation is the organising idea on the Beveridge side. Treat this as an entry point to the readings, not a claim that all arrangements within a family are identical.

The Netherlands readings focus on regulated insurer competition. Austria’s reports describe social-insurance and public actors sharing responsibilities. Italy and Norway both use tax-based arrangements, but the allocation of responsibilities between regions, municipalities and the state differs.

sections.title: Separate the functions
paragraphs: Ask four questions as a study method. Who raises money? How are risks and funds pooled? Who purchases or allocates care? Who delivers it? These questions prevent a private provider from being mistaken for a privately financed system, or a tax-based system from being mistaken for a system without contracts or activity incentives.

Read access separately: who is covered, which services are covered, which costs remain, and which organisational barriers affect use? The Italy and Austria reports are particularly useful for separating formal coverage from waiting, geography and private spending.

sections.title: A common comparison question
paragraphs: The course notice asks each country presentation to provide a short overview and address challenges created by patients moving to seek care elsewhere. An original preparation method is to ask how an outgoing or incoming patient flow could interact with the system’s purchaser, provider contracts, waiting times and budget.

Those questions are prompts for the guest session, not evidence that cross-border mobility has a measured effect of a particular size in each country. The supplied reports do not provide a comparable four-country dataset answering that question.

sections.title: Compare like with like
paragraphs: The readings are from different years and use different units. A spending amount in US-dollar purchasing-power parity cannot be ranked directly against an amount in euro purchasing-power parity without a consistent basis. Likewise, a share of all residents reporting unmet need differs from a share among people who reported needing care.
The comparison tool therefore uses qualitative, source-dated descriptions rather than a synthetic score for the best system. It is a revision aid, not a ranking or a live statistical dashboard.

sections.title: Follow money, decisions and services separately
paragraphs: The Bismarck/Beveridge table provides an organising model, but the country reports let you separate the actual functions. Revenue raising concerns where funds originate. Pooling concerns how resources are brought together. Purchasing and payment concern how money reaches providers. Delivery concerns who actually supplies services. An organisation can be privately owned while providing publicly financed care; similarly, tax-based finance does not establish that every clinician is a salaried public employee. The Italy and Austria reports contain mixed provider and payment arrangements that illustrate these distinctions.

Original comparison method: trace one treatment through the system and ask who sets entitlement, who pays, who provides the service and who can address a complaint or capacity gap. Then compare the same functions in the other country. This avoids comparing a financing label in one country with an ownership label in another. It also helps identify fragmentation: different bodies can each fulfil their own task while coordination between those tasks remains weak. This framework organises the readings; it does not rank the four countries.
sections.locator: Organizational issues, PDF p. 14; Italy 2024, PDF pp. 3–7; Austria 2024, PDF pp. 3–7

sections.title: Coverage, access and financial protection are not synonyms
paragraphs: Population coverage identifies who is included in a scheme. The benefits package identifies which services are included. Practical access asks whether covered people can obtain those services when and where they need them. Financial protection asks what burden remains for households. The Italian report discusses waiting and geographical barriers alongside nationally specified benefits, while the Austrian profile describes the choice between waiting for contracted care and paying for quicker private care. A high coverage figure therefore cannot by itself settle all four questions.

Original application: two patients may have the same formal entitlement yet face different travel distances, waiting times or ability to pay upfront. That observation supports an investigation of access, not an automatic conclusion that their legal entitlements differ. In a comparison answer, specify the outcome being evaluated and the population affected. A policy that improves an average may still leave a subgroup behind. The course’s rights, non-discrimination and values perspectives supply questions to ask of these system descriptions rather than a shortcut to a single “best system”.
sections.locator: Italy 2024, PDF pp. 6–7; Austria 2025, PDF pp. 14–15

sections.title: Read a reform as problem, mechanism, evidence and trade-off
paragraphs: The Norwegian chapter makes it possible to distinguish an intended mechanism from an observed result. Activity-based financing was introduced in a setting of long waiting times, but the chapter also describes additional funding, deficits and later coordination problems. The Dutch paper similarly explains the conditions needed for managed competition and calls the reform a work in progress. In both cases, “the reform aimed to improve efficiency” is not equivalent to “the reform achieved every intended outcome”.

A practical reading template is: identify the problem, describe which actor’s incentives or responsibilities changed, state what evidence the authors report, and retain the limitation or trade-off. For example, shorter hospital stays may coexist with a greater care burden outside the hospital in the Norwegian account. Do not treat a before-and-after line as proof of one causal mechanism, or a proposed adjustment as an implemented result. This method is an original study aid for comparing the assigned accounts without replacing their different findings.
sections.locator: Hagen & Feiring 2025, PDF pp. 4–9; van de Ven & Schut 2008, PDF pp. 5–6 and 16

units.title: The Netherlands: managed competition
units.intro: Read the 2007 overview, the 2008 design paper and the 2015 critique together. They tell a story about the conditions for competition—not an unqualified success claim.
review: These are historical readings, not a description of every current Dutch rule.
The 2006 reform combines mandatory basic insurance with regulated insurer choice.
Open enrolment and community rating interact with risk equalisation.
Insurers are intended to purchase care on behalf of members.
Quality information and governance are prerequisites, not optional extras.
Undercompensated predictable costs can leave incentives for risk selection.
Quality skimping is a risk discussed by the authors; not every cost reduction is selection.

sections.title: Why three readings?
paragraphs: Going Dutch is a concise perspective on the reform. The January 2008 draft adds the historical waves of coverage expansion, cost containment and managed competition, then explains institutional design. The 2015 article examines the incentives that can remain even when a risk-adjustment model looks sophisticated.

All three should be read in their publication context. Premiums, deductibles, market shares and forecasts in the older texts must not be shown as 2026 consumer guidance. Their durable teaching contribution is the relationship between incentives and safeguards.

sections.title: Competition needs a supporting system
paragraphs: The 2008 authors describe compulsory basic insurance, an annual choice of insurer, community-rated premiums and acceptance obligations for the basic contract. They also describe income-related support and risk-equalisation transfers. These mechanisms aim to combine choice with access and predictable funding for different risk groups.

They emphasise preconditions: risk equalisation, usable service classification and pricing, outcome and quality measurement, consumer information and effective governance. Without them, price competition is not the same as competition that improves care. Their account explicitly calls the reform a work in progress.

sections.title: Follow the incentive to the patient
paragraphs: In the 2015 analysis, an insurer may still expect a loss on some identifiable patient groups when compensation is below predictable expenditure. Selection can occur through how attractive a plan or its services are to those groups. The authors are particularly concerned about skimping on the quality of care needed by underpriced high-cost patients.

Do not equate higher clinical cost with inevitable unprofitability: the relevant comparison is expected cost against the compensation available for the person or group. The tool uses invented amounts to show this arithmetic and does not estimate any real insurer’s behaviour.

sections.title: Evaluate the evaluation
paragraphs: The article explains why an overall R-squared is not sufficient to establish that selection incentives have disappeared. It also warns that predictive ratios for groups already used in an ordinary-least-squares model can look reassuring by construction. The choice of subgroup and evaluation method is therefore part of the policy question.

Its proposed responses include improving adjusters and data, and risk sharing. The latter can reduce selection incentives while also weakening efficiency incentives. This is a trade-off to explain, not a problem solved by one universally optimal formula.

sections.title: The three waves explain why reform took time
paragraphs: The historical paper describes three broad waves: expansion towards universal coverage, government-led cost containment, and efficiency through managed competition. The sequence matters because the third wave responded to criticism of the incentives under earlier supply and price controls; it was not the first attempt to make care accessible. The authors describe a long transition rather than a one-day move from government to an unregulated market. Keep the approximate periods in the paper separate from claims about the Dutch system today.

The preconditions they identify include risk equalisation, workable product classification and pricing, quality and outcome measurement, usable consumer information and effective governance. These components perform different tasks. A choice of insurer is less useful without information; a low price is ambiguous without quality; accepting all applicants does not by itself remove incentives to avoid predictably costly groups. The lesson is about the interaction of institutions. The paper’s US comparison is a policy argument by its authors, not proof that an identical model can be transferred successfully to every country.
sections.locator: van de Ven & Schut, 24 January 2008 draft, PDF pp. 3–6

sections.title: Basic insurance, supplementary cover and selection incentives
paragraphs: The historical design distinguishes compulsory basic insurance from voluntary supplementary cover. Acceptance obligations and community rating for a basic product differ from the underwriting flexibility described for supplementary insurance. The paper also distinguishes income-related contributions, premiums paid to insurers, household subsidies and risk-equalisation transfers. These are not four names for the same payment. Subsidies address affordability for households; risk equalisation addresses the predicted cost composition of an insurer’s members.

The authors explain why supplementary products, group contracts and provider networks can interact with selection incentives. That is a mechanism to understand, not evidence that every insurer uses every possible strategy. The paper explicitly reports that some expected selection was not observed in the early transition period. Keep the distinction between possible incentives and demonstrated conduct. Its numerical premiums, deductibles, discounts and forecasts belong to the 2007/2008 setting and must not become practical advice about purchasing Dutch insurance now.
sections.locator: van de Ven & Schut 2008, PDF pp. 7–9 and 12–14; Going Dutch 2007, PDF pp. 2–3

sections.title: Predictive ratios: what a value close to one can hide
paragraphs: The article defines a group’s predictive ratio as average predicted expenditure divided by average actual expenditure. Below one indicates undercompensation in that evaluation; above one indicates overcompensation. However, the group’s definition matters. The authors warn that ratios for groups already represented by binary variables in an ordinary-least-squares model can be close to one by construction. Such a result does not show that unmodelled subgroups are adequately compensated. It is possible to report reassuring model statistics while important selection incentives remain.

The tables on PDF page 5 examine selected groups and distinguish the amount of under- or overcompensation from the reduction achieved by risk equalisation. A large reduction can coexist with a residual gap: improvement is not elimination. The table’s title, years and notes must remain attached to any discussion of its figures. Our numerical practice uses invented amounts rather than treating the table as current insurer data. It also keeps the article’s predictive ratio separate from the simpler expected-claims-margin calculator already available in Explore.
sections.locator: Risk Selection 2015, PDF pp. 4–5 (journal pp. 1715–1716)

units.title: Italy: universal coverage, regional delivery
units.intro: A source-dated guide to the 2024 Health System Summary. Focus on how a national entitlement is implemented across regional systems.
review: The 2024 report describes a decentralised National Health Service, the SSN.
The central level defines the national benefits package while regions organise delivery.
Taxation is the main funding source in the report.
GPs and paediatricians provide entry points and gatekeeping.
Public and accredited private providers can both deliver publicly funded care.
Regional variation and waiting times can limit practical access despite coverage.
The report’s reform directions are a 2024 snapshot, not verified completion claims.

sections.title: National entitlement, local implementation
paragraphs: The report describes an SSN with a nationally defined benefits package and regional responsibilities for financing, planning and service provision. National oversight and funding allocation coexist with regional implementation. The central question for the course is how shared commitments become available care in different places.

Local health authorities and different hospital organisations are involved in delivery. General practitioners and paediatricians are independent contractors acting as gatekeepers. Accredited private provision therefore does not contradict the report’s description of a national, tax-financed system.

sections.title: Money and provider incentives
paragraphs: The report describes national and regional taxes, pooling and an allocation formula taking population characteristics into account. Provider payment is mixed rather than uniform: it includes capitation, fees, diagnosis-related payments and budget lines. Distinguish the mechanism that allocates a region’s funds from the mechanism paying an individual provider.

Private spending is discussed largely through out-of-pocket payments, with voluntary insurance playing a smaller role. For analysis, ask which services generate patient spending and whether the expenditure reflects benefit gaps or barriers to using covered services. This guide does not provide current charges or registration advice.

sections.title: Coverage is not the end of the access question
paragraphs: The report identifies gaps and uneven availability in areas including dental and mental health care. It also describes waiting-time variation, regional differences and health-workforce pressures. A formally covered service can still be difficult to obtain locally or within an acceptable time.

It reports substantial mobility between Italian regions, often towards central and northern providers. That domestic pattern is not identical to the EU cross-border legal problem. It is, however, useful background for asking how patient flows interact with regional capacity and finance.

sections.title: Reform and a question for the country session
paragraphs: The 2024 source discusses strengthening primary and community care, telemedicine, integration and infrastructure through national reforms and the recovery plan. These are the report’s directions and implementation account at its reference date; they are not presented here as completed 2026 outcomes.

Original preparation question: if an entitlement is nationally guaranteed but the nearest appropriate service is far away, which part of AAAQ needs attention? Then distinguish geographical access from quality and from the separate issue of who pays when a patient uses another region or country.

sections.title: LEA and regional implementation: two levels of the same system
paragraphs: The report describes a national benefits package, the Livelli essenziali di assistenza (LEA), alongside regional responsibility for organisation and delivery. National pooling and regional allocation support that structure, while regions may provide additional services from their own resources. The distinction matters: common benefits do not imply identical local capacity or service arrangements. The report also describes local health authorities, hospital trusts, accredited private providers and independent GPs or paediatricians acting as gatekeepers.

An original way to read this structure is to separate a national commitment from the chain of decisions needed to fulfil it locally. Funding must be allocated, staff must be available and a provider must actually deliver the service. The report identifies interregional patient mobility as part of the financing picture. Do not assume that crossing a regional boundary within Italy and receiving care in another Member State are the same legal issue; one concerns the report’s domestic system account, while the other invokes the course’s cross-border framework.
sections.locator: Italy: Health System Summary 2024, PDF pp. 3–7

sections.title: Provider payment is more varied than a tax-financed label
paragraphs: The report separates how the SSN raises revenue from how providers are paid. Its payment overview includes capitation for local health authorities, combinations of capitation and fee-for-service for GPs, case-based hospital payments, and budget lines for activities not well captured by standard activity payments. These arrangements can coexist within one tax-financed system. Explaining only the revenue source would therefore miss the mechanisms by which organisations receive resources.

For study purposes, ask what unit triggers payment: an enrolled population, a service, a case or an allocated budget. Then ask which relevant work that payment unit might fail to describe. This second question is an analytical prompt, not a measured effect established for every Italian provider by the report. The reading notes that some activities use specific budget lines. It does not establish that one payment method always produces better quality, nor does it justify attributing all waiting-list differences to a single financial incentive.
sections.locator: Italy: Health System Summary 2024, PDF pp. 4 and 7

sections.title: A service can be included but still difficult to obtain
paragraphs: The report discusses dental and mental-health gaps, substantial variation in waiting lists and limited local availability in some areas. It also describes workforce pressures, including nursing shortages and uneven distribution. These findings should not be reduced to the claim that the SSN either covers everything or offers no protection. They identify different limitations affecting different services and populations within a broadly universal framework.

Original policy-reading exercise: consider a proposal to reduce waiting times by investing in community care. Separate the proposed facilities from the workforce, coordination and operating resources needed to use them. The report’s recovery-plan discussion supplies the context for investment, not a guarantee of future completion or equal benefit everywhere. A useful evaluation question would specify a service, a region, the relevant patient group and a time period. Do not present national reform targets or anticipated workforce changes as verified 2026 outcomes.
sections.locator: Italy: Health System Summary 2024, PDF pp. 7–8 and 14–15

units.title: Norway: incentives, priorities & accountability
units.intro: Follow the 2025 chapter’s argument: expand activity and access, coordinate services, and make the allocation of scarce resources explicit.
review: The chapter describes a tax-financed, semi-decentralised system.
Municipalities and the state-owned regional specialist-care structures have different responsibilities.
Global budgets coexist with activity incentives; these are not mutually exclusive models.
Reforms include GP lists, hospital choice, state hospital ownership and coordination.
Priority setting considers expected benefit, severity and cost-effectiveness.
Clinical and group-level priority decisions use the criteria differently.
Returning to square one is a concern discussed by the authors, not a confirmed outcome.

sections.title: Start with the division of responsibilities
paragraphs: Hagen and Feiring describe municipal responsibility for primary, social and long-term care, and state administration of specialist care through regional health authorities. Their focus is efficient and fair resource use rather than an exhaustive guide to all services.

The municipal level allocates resources across several public functions and between forms of care. The specialist system uses predominantly budget-based financing with additional economic incentives. The coexistence of these mechanisms is central to the chapter’s account.

sections.title: What the reforms attempted
paragraphs: The chapter discusses activity-based hospital financing, the GP list system, hospital choice, state takeover of hospitals and coordination between levels. It reports improvements in activity or access alongside problems such as deficits, workload, fragmented responsibilities and concern about early discharge.

Read outcomes measure by measure. For example, the coordination package includes more than one incentive, and the authors report that not all components produced the intended effects. It would be misleading to label the entire package simply a success or a failure.

sections.title: Priority setting is both technical and normative
paragraphs: The chapter identifies expected benefit, severity and cost-effectiveness as central criteria. It distinguishes clinical-level judgment from group-level health technology assessment, including the use of quality-adjusted life years and absolute shortfall in the latter context.

A cost-effectiveness calculation does not remove the need to justify which outcomes matter, who bears the opportunity cost and how severity enters the decision. The chapter describes institutional procedures for managing these decisions, rather than offering a universal funding threshold.

sections.title: Who is accountable for a difficult decision?
paragraphs: Delegation to expert bodies can create consistency and protect decisions from short-term pressures. The authors also discuss the risk that politically and ethically contested questions become treated as merely technical, reducing public or elected influence.

Their concluding concern is that scaling back incentives while demand and workforce pressures remain might revive waiting-time and priority-setting difficulties. This is the authors’ argument about a risk, not proof that the system has already returned to an earlier state. An original seminar question is how to preserve expertise while keeping decisions transparent and contestable.

sections.title: Activity and budgets: two sides of the financing story
paragraphs: The chapter links activity-based financing from 1997 to increased treatment activity and later reductions in waiting, while also identifying increased budgets, supplementary funding and deficits. It reports costs of the arrangement as well as gains: dependence on central funding, demands for additional resources and disputes about responsibility. This balanced account prevents the simplified conclusion that paying for more cases automatically solves a capacity problem without creating another challenge.

The later discussion describes criticism of economic management and a proposal to return more strongly to global budgets, followed by a more limited change in the activity-based component. Preserve the difference between a commission’s proposal and the government response described by the authors. The chapter’s question about returning to earlier problems is an analytical concern, not a prediction that must have come true. When writing an answer, identify both the incentives for activity and the mechanisms for controlling total expenditure.
sections.locator: Hagen & Feiring 2025, PDF pp. 4 and 7

sections.title: Coordination reform: evaluate each component separately
paragraphs: The 2012 coordination package is presented as a response to fragmented services, insufficient prevention and changing needs. The chapter distinguishes investment incentives for municipal acute wards, municipal co-financing of hospital treatment, and municipal payment for patients ready for discharge. These instruments targeted different behaviours. Their results should not be merged into a single verdict about whether “coordination reform worked”.

The authors report a reduction in some acute admissions associated with municipal acute wards, no significant admissions effect from the co-financing initiative, and shorter stays accompanied by concerns about the burden of early discharge. They also describe health communities and explicitly note that this initiative had not yet been evaluated in their account. An original evaluation should retain that absence of evidence. Reduced hospital use is one outcome; appropriate rehabilitation and municipal capacity are separate questions rather than benefits that can be assumed from the same statistic.
sections.locator: Hagen & Feiring 2025, PDF pp. 7–8

sections.title: Priority setting: clinical judgment versus group decisions
paragraphs: The chapter describes expected benefit, severity and cost-effectiveness as three main criteria. It distinguishes textually expressed criteria and discretion at the clinical level from quantified assessment at the group level. In the latter setting, benefit is described using QALYs and severity through absolute shortfall. The use of these measures does not mean that the lowest-cost option automatically wins, or that one metric replaces the other criteria.

The technology-introduction system also involves institutions, roles and decisions: health technology assessment informs the process, while the described Decision Forum has authority over introduction or disinvestment. The authors connect this structure with safety, equality, transparency and accountability, but note limited knowledge about some outcomes. A strong answer therefore explains both the evidence and who makes the decision. Avoid inventing a willingness-to-pay threshold or a patient-level entitlement that the supplied extract does not establish.
sections.locator: Hagen & Feiring 2025, PDF pp. 8–9

units.title: Austria: access, fragmentation & reform
units.intro: Use the 2024 structure report and the 2025 profile as complementary snapshots. Keep their underlying years and indicator definitions visible.
review: The reports describe shared responsibilities across federal, regional and social-insurance actors.
Financing combines social-insurance contributions and taxation.
The system has a strong specialist and hospital orientation in these readings.
Near-universal coverage can coexist with regional or financial barriers.
Contracted and non-contracted doctors create different access and payment experiences.
Digital investment alone does not establish widespread effective use.
Do not calculate a trend from indicators with different denominators.

sections.title: One system, multiple centres of responsibility
paragraphs: The 2024 summary describes federal regulation, Länder hospital responsibilities, and self-governing social-insurance and provider bodies involved in ambulatory care. Funding combines compulsory insurance contributions with tax resources. This structure creates coordination challenges across institutions and care settings.

The report describes joint planning and target-based governance as responses to fragmentation. The analytical task is to connect the governance arrangement to the patient pathway: where do responsibilities change hands, and can the financial incentives encourage shifting costs elsewhere?

sections.title: Good aggregate access can conceal unequal experience
paragraphs: Both reports describe very broad coverage. The 2025 profile nevertheless discusses a wait-or-pay dilemma: use a contracted provider with possible delays, or pay more for access to a non-contracted provider. It also identifies geographical and specialty imbalances behind apparently high overall physician availability.

These are not contradictions. Coverage, waiting, financial protection and workforce distribution are different dimensions. Use them together rather than using a national doctor-density figure to conclude that every locality has sufficient publicly accessible care.

sections.title: Rebalancing services and making digital systems useful
paragraphs: The sources discuss strengthening primary and ambulatory services and reducing reliance on inpatient care. The 2025 profile describes substantial health-ICT investment while also identifying gaps in use and implementation of ELGA. A budget allocation is an input; useful access and coordinated care are outcomes.

Its pharmaceutical section distinguishes outpatient reimbursement and pricing from hospital procurement and high-cost medicine pressures. These sectors should not be merged into a single assertion about whether medicines are cheap or expensive. The report’s findings remain tied to its reference period.

sections.title: An indicator-reading exercise
paragraphs: The 2024 summary reports unmet medical need for the population. The 2025 profile explicitly reports a measure among people who experienced medical need. The comparison of those percentages is not automatically a before-and-after trend, because the denominator differs.

Original seminar prompt: name one measure of formal coverage, one of effective access and one of financial protection that you would inspect before evaluating a reform. State the population and year for each. The supplied readings support this method but not a single composite score for Austria.

sections.title: Fragmentation is a relationship between responsibilities
paragraphs: The report describes responsibilities distributed across the federal government, Länder, insurance funds and provider bodies. Its financing overview combines contributions, taxation and private payments, while its provider overview separates hospital and ambulatory arrangements. Fragmentation here concerns the way these responsibilities interact; it is not simply a count of institutions. A reform involving one payer or one service sector may depend on decisions made elsewhere in the system.

Target-based governance is presented as an attempt to improve joint planning and coordination, bringing the principal actors into a common process. The report also describes consolidation of insurance funds without claiming that every benefit and regional payment difference disappeared. Read organisational change and service change separately. A new structure can create a mechanism for cooperation, but the existence of that structure alone is not evidence that every problem of continuity, financing or resource allocation has been resolved.
sections.locator: Austria: Health System Summary 2024, PDF pp. 3–7 and 13–14

sections.title: Wait or pay: interpret the household’s actual choice
paragraphs: The profile describes broad coverage alongside growth in non-contracted private practice and uneven availability of publicly contracted doctors. It links this with a choice between waiting for a covered appointment and paying for potentially quicker access. A reimbursement percentage must be read against its base: the report describes reimbursement relative to an SHI tariff for an equivalent contracted service, not automatically a fixed fraction of the private invoice. This distinction matters when explaining why a financial burden can remain.

The workforce discussion reinforces the same point. A high national physician density does not establish that the right specialty is available locally under an insurance contract. The profile describes geographic and contractual imbalances, so an access argument should identify which providers and which population it concerns. This is a reading of the 2025 report, not personalised reimbursement advice. Do not use the report’s figures to estimate what a student will pay for a current appointment without checking the relevant service and institution.
sections.locator: Austria: Country Health Profile 2025, PDF pp. 9–11 and 14–15

sections.title: Investment, uptake and outcomes: three different measures
paragraphs: The digital-health discussion contrasts substantial investment with implementation and uptake difficulties. Spending on infrastructure, the presence of records in ELGA, use by providers and use by residents are different measures. One cannot substitute for another. The profile discusses governance and information gaps, which explains why buying technology alone is not the entire implementation problem. A later mandate or plan in the report should retain its reported status rather than being treated as proof that adoption subsequently became complete.

The pharmaceutical section offers another useful comparison within the system: nationally coordinated outpatient reimbursement and pricing are contrasted with more fragmented hospital procurement of expensive medicines. The report discusses a new appraisal board and the limits of generic and biosimilar uptake. These observations support questions about governance and coordination, not a claim that every medicine is managed through one identical process. Keep policy descriptions, reported performance and reform ambitions in separate sentences so the evidence for each remains visible.
sections.locator: Austria: Country Health Profile 2025, PDF pp. 17–20

units.title: European Health Union: from analysis to proposals
units.intro: Bring the four legal and ethical perspectives into a policy discussion. Keep the present framework separate from the future you are proposing.
review: The workshop connects the course title to groups, needs, resources and levels of responsibility.
The European Health Union is presented as a collection of related initiatives, not one insurance scheme.
De lege lata and de lege ferenda distinguish the existing framework from proposed change.
The 2006 health values and the manifesto have different roles in the preparation.
The lecturer’s newer values framework is presented as a proposal.
One Health connects the human, animal and environmental perspectives in the workshop.
A defensible proposal should identify implementation, trade-offs and who is accountable.

sections.title: Why end with a workshop?
paragraphs: The workshop revisits the historical development of European health action and asks what the right to health means for current and future challenges. Its course-title diagram asks which groups have needs, which resources are involved, where they should be provided and by which level.

The diagram includes more than money: it also asks about analogue and digital resources, vulnerable groups, social and commercial determinants, and the relationship between health and other policies. It is an agenda for analysis, not an invitation to assume all priorities have already been settled.

sections.title: An umbrella of initiatives
paragraphs: The deck groups cross-border health threats, institutional roles, cancer, pharmaceuticals, health data, mental health and global health under the EHU discussion. Its timelines contain both enacted measures and proposals from different periods.

When using a timeline entry in an answer, identify whether it is a proposal, an adopted instrument or an implementation milestone. A policy initiative’s presence in the diagram is not evidence that every part was operational at the date of the class. This edition does not silently update historical slides into a current legislative tracker.

sections.title: Read the two preparation documents differently
paragraphs: The lecturer assigns the 2006 Council conclusions and the European Health Union manifesto. The conclusions articulate common health-system values and operating principles while recognising different national arrangements. The manifesto is a document advocating a direction for a Health Union.

Critical reading does not require agreement with every proposal or a signature. Ask what each document says should be protected, what institutional change it implies, and what trade-offs it leaves unresolved. The Hub’s workshop sheet is an original preparation aid, not the lecturer’s assessment rubric.

sections.title: Existing framework versus proposed future
paragraphs: The final slides present four proposals: reframe the values around a Health Union, add a purpose-driven preamble, articulate a cumulative set of core values, and connect those values to action-guiding principles. Their proposed set includes dignity, freedom and autonomy, universal access, equity, resilience and solidarity.

The deck attributes these proposals to a 2026 publication. This study edition identifies them as proposals reported in the deck, without claiming independent review of the cited article or that the values have been adopted as new binding law. Use the workshop builder to specify a population, a problem, a value, practical action, a trade-off and an accountable actor.

sections.title: History explains the workshop’s institutional question
paragraphs: The workshop traces gradual development rather than presenting European health cooperation as beginning with COVID-19. It contrasts early ambitious proposals, including the White Pool, with the later step-by-step development of public-health competences, institutions and instruments. Its timeline connects crises and institutional responses, but the sequence alone is not evidence that each crisis uniquely caused each legal change. Some examples are explicitly unsuccessful proposals or historical instruments.

The diagram also mixes legal categories: a treaty, a regulation, a communication, an agency and a policy initiative are not interchangeable. An original revision exercise is to classify an item before explaining its role. This preserves the lecture’s difference between institutional change and a substantive programme such as cancer policy. It also prevents the phrase “European Health Union” from being mistaken for a single law that establishes one uniform national service across all participating countries.
sections.locator: European Health Union workshop, PDF pp. 3–8

sections.title: Read the four proposals as a coherent package
paragraphs: The workshop’s proposed update has four connected components: reframing values around a European Health Union, adding a purpose-driven preamble, articulating a concise set of core values, and linking values to operational principles. The proposed values include dignity, freedom and autonomy, universal access, equity, resilience and solidarity. The deck presents them as cumulative and non-hierarchical, not a menu from which a policymaker chooses whichever value is most convenient.

The accompanying diagram links principles such as patient engagement, privacy, quality and safety, accountability and redress, non-discrimination, and evidence- and ethics-based care. The deck treats dignity and solidarity as having overarching importance rather than assigning them a single narrow operational link. These are the proposals as presented in the slides, not a claim that they have become binding law. The article cited on the slide has not been reviewed independently here; attribution remains to the supplied workshop material.
sections.locator: European Health Union workshop, PDF pp. 24–26

sections.title: Build an argument across needs, resources and society
paragraphs: The course-title diagram asks whose needs matter, which resources are needed, where they are supplied and at what level, and how health relates to society. It includes digital and non-digital resources and social and commercial determinants. The later One Health diagram links humans, animals and environment. These prompts broaden the policy discussion beyond the immediate treatment bill without supplying a single preferred answer to every question.

Original workshop method: define a problem for a specific group, distinguish the existing framework from the proposed change, explain the relevant value and principle, identify the responsible actor and resources, and anticipate a trade-off. Finish with evidence that would help assess the proposal and a limitation you cannot resolve from the readings. A student may reasonably defend different policies if the reasoning is transparent. Signing a manifesto is separate from understanding it; this study aid does not require agreement with the initiative or manufacture a lecturer-approved position.
sections.locator: European Health Union workshop, PDF pp. 10 and 17–26

glossary.definition: Treaties and the Charter form the foundational legal layer presented in the course.
Instruments such as regulations, directives and decisions, distinguished from the Treaties.
Creating similar legal standards across national systems, rather than only removing a barrier.
The recipient crosses the border to receive a service; patient mobility is the course example.
Permission considered before treatment under a relevant route; its conditions depend on the legal basis.
An examination of whether an interference or restriction is appropriate and necessary for its legitimate objective, within the relevant framework.
Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union; distinct from the ECHR.
European Convention on Human Rights, in the Council of Europe system.
Availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality: a framework discussed through General Comment 14.
Three related types of obligation: avoid interference, prevent third-party interference, and take measures to realise the right.
An explicit use of the relevant protected ground in different treatment.
A neutral-looking criterion can disadvantage a protected group; the legal framework, effects and evidence matter.
In the health-values discussion, access according to need rather than ability to pay or irrelevant personal characteristics.
A commitment connected in the course to shared protection, financing and accessibility.
More concrete ways to act on values, including safety, participation, redress and confidentiality.
A regulated institutional approach combining insurer choice with safeguards, information and purchasing incentives in the historical Dutch readings.
Transfers designed to offset predictable risk-related differences and support intended cross-subsidies.
The article’s concern that services for undercompensated groups may be made less attractive or of poorer quality.
A budget allocation considered alongside additional activity incentives in the Norwegian chapter.
Explicit choices between competing uses of scarce resources; the Norwegian chapter discusses benefit, severity and cost-effectiveness.
An entry or referral role for primary-care providers in the relevant system; its arrangements differ by country.
Direct household expenditure on care, separate from population insurance coverage.

glossary.term: De lege lata / de lege ferenda
glossary.definition: The existing legal framework / proposals for future change.
The interconnected human, animal and environmental perspective used in the workshop.

cases.title: A waiting-list refusal is not the whole answer
cases.scenario: A fictional patient is told that planned surgery abroad cannot be authorised because everyone must wait their turn at home. The administrator supplies no individual medical assessment. Analyse which questions the lecture’s patient-mobility chart would require you to separate.
cases.locator: Economic rights, PDF pp. 21 and 25; original scenario, not the facts of Watts

steps.title: Identify the legal route
steps.text: The scenario does not say whether the patient seeks an S2 authorisation, reimbursement under the Directive or a Treaty-based remedy. Identify the route before borrowing conditions from it.

steps.title: Separate entitlement from waiting
steps.text: Ask whether the home system covers the treatment, what general conditions apply, and what the patient’s clinical circumstances are. The lecture treats waiting through a medical rather than merely administrative perspective.

steps.title: Examine the procedure
steps.text: Ask whether the decision is reasoned, accessible to the patient and open to review. The chart’s procedural protections are distinct from its reimbursement discussion.

cases.conclusion: The administrator’s sentence is not a complete source-based analysis. More facts and an individual assessment are needed; this does not establish automatic authorisation or full reimbursement.
cases.trap: Do not promise a refund of the entire foreign bill merely because waiting exists.

check.question: What is the most defensible next analytical step?
options: Assume all treatment abroad is covered
Identify the route and the individual clinical assessment
Ignore the home benefit package
check.explanation: The lecture distinguishes coverage, route, medical delay and procedural questions.

cases.title: Three cases, not one vaccination verdict
cases.scenario: Compare the supplied discussion of Široká, Padova and Vavřička. A classmate writes: “The European courts approved compulsory vaccination in all three cases.” Explain why this statement loses important distinctions.

steps.title: Read the procedural outcome
steps.text: Široká is used to teach the Charter’s scope and the absence of jurisdiction in the questions presented. Padova is used to highlight an inadequately supported reference and its connection to EU law.

steps.title: Identify the rights framework
steps.text: Vavřička is the lecture’s detailed Article 8 ECHR analysis. It is not a CFR judgment by the same court as the CJEU cases.

steps.title: Keep reasoning and facts together
steps.text: The Article 8 sequence considers interference, legal basis, legitimate aim, necessity and safeguards. The absence of forced administration and the other specific safeguards matter.

cases.conclusion: A procedural obstacle is not a merits ruling. The comparison should identify the court, instrument, question reached and limited conclusion in each source account.
cases.trap: Do not turn inadmissibility or lack of jurisdiction into a universal endorsement of a public-health policy.

check.question: Which finding differs from a substantive proportionality assessment?
options: A conclusion on the applicable safeguards
A conclusion on necessity in a democratic society
A finding that the Court lacks jurisdiction
