check.explanation: Jurisdiction determines whether the court can address the questions; it is not the same as deciding their substantive justification.

cases.title: Who loses out under a neutral-looking rule?
cases.scenario: A fictional hospital gives an optional training opportunity only to full-time employees. Its review team has not yet examined the composition of the excluded group. Apply the structure of the short summary without assuming facts that are not supplied.
cases.locator: Non-discrimination short summary, PDF pp. 1–4; original training scenario

steps.title: Name the criterion and comparator
steps.text: The rule explicitly distinguishes working hours. Identify the relevant comparison and the protected ground that might be indirectly affected; do not simply rename working hours as sex.

steps.title: Ask for evidence
steps.text: The short summary conditions its staff-event analysis on statistics about differential impact. Here, the group composition and effect must be established rather than asserted.

steps.title: Examine the aim and alternatives
steps.text: What is the actual purpose of the full-time requirement? Could another arrangement meet that purpose with less exclusion? Apply the appropriate framework rather than assuming every distinction is prohibited.

cases.conclusion: An indirect-discrimination concern is plausible, but the scenario alone does not prove the necessary effect or settle justification.
cases.trap: “Neutral wording” does not prove equal effects, and a possible unequal effect is not a substitute for evidence.

check.question: What missing information is central to the analysis?
options: The rule’s distributional effect on a relevant protected group
Only whether the rule names a protected characteristic
Only the manager’s stated lack of discriminatory intent
check.explanation: The supplied short summary explicitly links its example to evidence of disproportionate impact.

cases.title: A digital service with an equity slogan
cases.scenario: A fictional health service proposes app-only appointment booking. The team claims that faster booking proves the policy respects equity. Use the lecture’s value-to-principle diagram to develop a fuller argument.
cases.locator: Values and ethics, PDF pp. 8 and 26–30; original digital scenario

steps.title: Separate the commitment from the outcome
steps.text: Equity is a broad value. Faster booking is a particular outcome and does not establish that access has improved for every relevant group.

steps.title: Make the principle operational
steps.text: Consider patient involvement, information, privacy and non-discrimination. An assisted or non-digital route is an original design option to assess, not a requirement quoted from the slide.

steps.title: Identify accountability
steps.text: Who listens to excluded users, reviews booking errors and evaluates practical access? Explain an actual process rather than adding more value labels.

cases.conclusion: A stronger proposal connects the value with an action, an affected group, a safeguard and evidence. The lecture does not provide one automatic solution to the fictional design problem.
cases.trap: Do not treat a value as an outcome measure or treat efficient administration as proof of fairness.

check.question: Which addition best strengthens the reasoning?
options: A count of registrations that excludes people unable to register
The adoption of a privacy policy without examining access
A way to evaluate access for people unable to use the app
check.explanation: The diagram’s move towards practical principles encourages an explanation of implementation and affected groups.

cases.title: Two coverage figures, two different experiences
cases.scenario: Two fictional regions report the same high insurance-coverage rate. One has long travel distances; the other has short travel distances but large household payments for the service being studied. What can and cannot be concluded?
cases.locator: Italy 2024, PDF pp. 6–7; Austria 2025, PDF pp. 14–15; original regions

steps.title: Define the metric
steps.text: The coverage rate concerns inclusion in the scheme. It does not tell you the exact benefit package, service availability or financial burden.

steps.title: Separate the barriers
steps.text: Travel and affordability are different dimensions of access. Compare the same service, patient population and time period before drawing conclusions.

steps.title: Choose evidence for the question
steps.text: Travel time, waiting, household costs and reported unmet needs would address different aspects. These are original evaluation suggestions; the scenario supplies none of their actual values.

cases.conclusion: Equal coverage is compatible with different practical barriers. There is not enough information to identify a single better region or calculate an overall quality score.
cases.trap: Do not use coverage, accessibility and financial protection as interchangeable labels.

check.question: Which conclusion is supported?
options: The two regions necessarily have identical access
Different access barriers may remain despite equal coverage
The region with shorter travel must always be better
check.explanation: The reports distinguish formal coverage from access and remaining household burdens.

cases.title: The reassuring average that misses a subgroup
cases.scenario: In an invented evaluation, one subgroup has average predicted expenditure of €3,600 and average actual expenditure of €4,000. A second reported model statistic looks strong. Interpret the ratio without claiming that either number comes from the 2015 tables.
cases.locator: Risk Selection 2015, PDF pp. 4–5; all euro amounts in this case are invented

steps.title: Calculate the stated ratio
steps.text: Divide predicted by actual average expenditure: 3,600 / 4,000 = 0.90. This is a dimensionless ratio, not a 90-euro reimbursement.

steps.title: Interpret the gap
steps.text: In this illustration the prediction is €400 below the subgroup’s actual mean. The article associates undercompensation of identifiable groups with selection incentives; it does not equate an incentive with proven conduct.

steps.title: Question the evaluation
steps.text: Ask how the subgroup was defined and whether it simply reproduces model variables. The authors warn that favourable fit measures or constructed group ratios do not exclude residual incentives elsewhere.

cases.conclusion: The group ratio indicates underprediction in this example. It does not identify the firm’s realised profit, prove discrimination by a named insurer or describe current Dutch expenditure.
cases.trap: A predictive ratio and the compensation-minus-claims calculator are different quantities.

check.question: What is the predictive ratio for this invented group?
check.explanation: Average predicted expenditure divided by average actual expenditure is 3,600 / 4,000 = 0.90.

cases.title: National benefits, a local queue
cases.scenario: A fictional patient is entitled to a service in the national package but cannot obtain a timely local appointment. A policy memo concludes that the service is therefore absent from the national package. Use the Italy report to critique the conclusion.
cases.locator: Italy: Health System Summary 2024, PDF pp. 3–8; original patient scenario

steps.title: Identify the level of the claim
steps.text: The national package describes entitlement. The report gives regions and local authorities major roles in organising actual provision.

steps.title: Locate the access problem
steps.text: Availability, waiting, staffing and geography can prevent timely use of a covered service. Those are implementation questions, not automatic evidence that the benefit has been removed.

steps.title: Match the proposed remedy to the problem
steps.text: A change to the package is different from a change to capacity or organisation. Ask what evidence identifies the bottleneck before choosing a response.

cases.conclusion: The memo confuses formal inclusion with practical access. The patient’s difficulty is important, but the scenario does not establish that the national package excludes the service.
cases.trap: Do not infer the legal benefit package from a waiting-list observation alone.

check.question: Which distinction is essential?
options: Formal entitlement versus place of insurance enrolment
Formal entitlement versus timely provision
Public financing versus the complete absence of private providers
check.explanation: The report separates the nationally specified package from regional delivery and practical barriers.

cases.title: A shorter stay that shifts the burden
cases.scenario: A fictional reform review celebrates shorter hospital stays after changing discharge-related payments. It does not measure the care available after discharge. Apply the cautions in the Norwegian chapter.
cases.locator: Hagen & Feiring 2025, PDF pp. 7–8; original review scenario

steps.title: Identify the mechanism
steps.text: The chapter distinguishes discharge-ready patient payments from other coordination measures. State which actor faces a changed incentive and what outcome is being measured.

steps.title: Look across the service boundary
steps.text: Shorter stays may reduce hospital use while increasing municipal responsibilities. The chapter reports concerns about premature discharge and rehabilitation.

steps.title: Retain uncertainty
steps.text: Ask about subsequent care, municipal capacity and patient experience. The fictional review supplies no evidence of those outcomes, so they cannot be assumed to have improved.

cases.conclusion: The reported result may be one improvement, but it is not by itself a complete assessment of coordinated or appropriate care.
cases.trap: Do not count work moved outside a hospital as work that has disappeared from the health system.

check.question: Which evidence would address the missing part of the evaluation?
options: Hospital discharge volume without measuring subsequent care
The national hospital budget alone
Availability and adequacy of follow-up care
check.explanation: The chapter discusses the burden on municipalities and possible rehabilitation problems alongside shorter stays.

cases.title: Eighty per cent of what?
cases.scenario: Use an invented private fee of €150 and an invented equivalent SHI tariff of €80. A classmate applies the profile’s described 80% tariff-based reimbursement directly to the private invoice. Demonstrate the arithmetic distinction, not a real claim entitlement.
cases.locator: Austria: Country Health Profile 2025, PDF p. 14; invented fees, no individual reimbursement advice

steps.title: Identify the base
steps.text: The profile describes reimbursement by reference to the SHI tariff for an equivalent contracted service, not automatically the non-contracted provider’s invoice.

steps.title: Calculate the illustration
steps.text: Eighty per cent of the invented €80 tariff is €64. Against the invented €150 fee, the difference is €86. Applying 80% directly to €150 would instead produce €120 and uses the wrong base for this illustration.

steps.title: State the limit
steps.text: A real reimbursement depends on the applicable institution, service and conditions. The example does not establish eligibility, supplementary-cover terms or current tariff amounts.

cases.conclusion: The base of a percentage is part of its meaning. A tariff-based percentage can leave more out-of-pocket spending than a reader expects from the percentage alone.
cases.trap: Never turn an illustrative calculation into a promise about a student’s actual appointment bill.

check.question: In this explicitly invented example, what is 80% of the tariff?
check.explanation: The stipulated tariff is €80, so 0.8 × 80 = €64; €86 is the remaining difference, not reimbursement.

cases.title: A proposal is not an enacted rule
cases.scenario: A student proposes an access policy and writes that the six values on the workshop’s final diagram are already a new binding EU legal instrument. Use the deck’s organisation to improve the claim.
cases.locator: European Health Union workshop, PDF pp. 2, 17 and 24–26

steps.title: Identify the section’s status
steps.text: The agenda distinguishes de lege lata from de lege ferenda. The final diagram belongs to the proposals for future development.

steps.title: Explain the proposal faithfully
steps.text: The deck links an EHU framing, a preamble, cumulative core values and operational principles. It does not present six isolated alternatives from which only one should be selected.

steps.title: Separate argument from authority
steps.text: The student can argue that the proposal would strengthen the policy. That argument is different from asserting that a binding instrument already requires the measure.

cases.conclusion: Present the proposal as a proposal, explain how it guides the policy and identify what further legal and practical work would be needed.
cases.trap: An academic proposal can be influential without already being enacted law.

check.question: Which label fits the final proposed values framework in the deck?
options: A reform proposal presented for discussion
An already binding extension of Article 2 TEU
A replacement for every national benefits package
check.explanation: The deck explicitly places the final framework in the future-oriented proposal section.

cases.title: An AAAQ diagnosis with more than one barrier
cases.scenario: A fictional rural clinic exists and has competent clinicians, but appointments require a long trip, fees are unaffordable for some households, and information is not provided in a usable form. Classify the barriers without assuming that one label exhausts the case.
cases.locator: Human rights, PDF pp. 23–24; original clinic scenario

steps.title: Use the dimensions precisely
steps.text: Travel, affordability and information correspond to physical, economic and information accessibility. The clinic’s existence alone does not settle all AAAQ dimensions.

steps.title: Do not invent another failure
steps.text: The scenario describes competent clinicians; it does not establish poor scientific quality. Additional quality or acceptability problems might exist, but they have not been supplied.

steps.title: Connect the analysis with responsibility
steps.text: The respect–protect–fulfil framework asks what duties and actors might address the barriers. The source provides the framework, not the clinic’s actual governance or a definitive remedy.

cases.conclusion: Several accessibility barriers are supported by the scenario. Use them as a starting point for a more precise investigation rather than automatically assigning every AAAQ label.
cases.trap: Do not infer poor quality from distance alone or assume that one barrier excludes all others.

check.question: Which set most directly matches the supplied facts?
options: Only quality and nothing else
Only clinic quantity
Physical, economic and information accessibility
check.explanation: These are three distinct accessibility dimensions listed in the lecture’s AAAQ slide.

cases.title: Language proficiency for the actual job
cases.scenario: A fictional hospital advertises a role involving a fixed set of routine logistics tasks and demands native-level language proficiency. The advertisement does not explain why that level is required. Analyse the requirement using the short summary.
cases.locator: Non-discrimination short summary, PDF pp. 1 and 3–4; original logistics scenario

steps.title: Separate the rule from its possible effect
steps.text: The condition is expressed as language proficiency, not nationality. Ask whether it may disadvantage a relevant group in practice; neutral wording alone does not settle this.

steps.title: Test the job-related need
steps.text: The short summary accepts that sufficient language ability may be necessary. Identify the tasks, communication demands and safety needs before deciding whether the advertised level is excessive.

steps.title: Consider an alternative
steps.text: A job-relevant proficiency assessment is an original option to examine. Its adequacy must be evaluated rather than assumed, and the relevant legal framework must still be identified.

cases.conclusion: The source supports scrutiny of an exaggerated requirement, not a rule that hospitals may never require language proficiency.
cases.trap: Do not confuse a safety-related communication need with an unexplained demand for perfect language.

check.question: What does the short summary most directly ask the reader to examine?
options: Whether every language requirement is automatically unlawful
Whether the required level is necessary for the particular work
Whether nationality and language are always identical
check.explanation: The explanation distinguishes sufficient command for the job from an exaggerated level.
